https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/17/leng.text: Menü Kereső A lengyel buszbaleset 22 sérültjét hétfő éjszaka szállítják haza Belföld Dévai László Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hétfő éjszaka 22 sérültet szállítanak haza Lengyelországba az M3-as autópályán történt súlyos buszbaleset után – közölte Katarzyna Kacperczyk lengyel egészségügyi miniszterhelyettes Miskolcon, írja az MTI. A betegeket Debrecenből egy speciális állami repülőgéppel viszik Rzeszówba. A döntést a magyar orvosokkal közösen hozták meg, a sérülteket rendőri segítséggel, konvojban szállítják a debreceni repülőtérre. Tizennyolc sérült egyelőre Magyarországon marad, öten pedig már elhagyták az országot, róluk a családjuk gondoskodik. Két beteg esetében még nem döntöttek arról, hogy állapotuk lehetővé teszi-e az éjszakai hazaszállítást. A lengyel Humanitárius-Orvosi Segítségnyújtási Csoport mind a négy érintett magyarországi kórházban jelen van, és a következő napokban folytatnák a sérültek hazaszállítását. A legsúlyosabb sérülteket Miskolcon kezelik. A kórházba vasárnap 11 beteget vittek, közülük hárman azóta távozhattak, nyolcan azonban továbbra is az intézményben vannak. Ketten az intenzív osztályon fekszenek súlyos, életveszélyes állapotban, egyiküket hétfőn is műtötték. Öt beteget a traumatológián, egyet pedig az idegsebészeten kezelnek. A baleset halálos áldozatainak hazaszállítását a lengyel konzulátus szervezi. A miskolci kórházba 11 elhunytat szállítottak, közülük hatot pedig már azonosítottak . Kacperczyk szerint már megkezdődött a szükséges konzuli és adminisztratív ügyintézés is. Közben újabb utasok szólaltak meg a vasárnap hajnali lengyel buszbalesettel kapcsolatban, egyikük azt mondta: az emberek azonnal elkezdtek segíteni egymásnak. Az egyik fiatal zarándok állítólag kitört egy nyílást, amelyen keresztül megkezdhették a sérültek kimentését. A TVN24-nek nyilatkozó túlélő arról beszélt, hogy lábfájdalom miatt a busz padlóján feküdt, és egyszer csak nyugtalanító hangot hallott. A lengyel zarándokokat szállító busz augusztus 16-án hajnalban borult az oldalára az M3-as autópályán. A járművön 59-en utaztak, közülük 12-en meghaltak , többen súlyosan megsérültek. A sérülteket Miskolcra, Debrecenbe, Nyíregyházára és Egerbe vitték. A rendőrség halálos tömegszerencsétlenség gondatlan okozása miatt indított eljárást a sofőr ellen, akit őrizetbe vettek; letartóztatásáról a bíróság dönthet. https://www.lawtimesnews.com/practice-ar.text: CONTINUE TO SITE CONTINUE TO SITE Andreea Muth joins WeirFoulds as a new partner After more than seven years at Pallett Valo, Muth strengthens WeirFoulds’ wills, trusts and estates group Former Pallett Valo partner Andreea Muth has joined WeirFoulds as a wills, trusts and estates partner, working from Toronto and Oakville. Muth brings to WeirFoulds her business owner estate planning-focused practice. She has tackled estate, succession, tax, and wealth planning matters on behalf of business owners, entrepreneurs, families, and private clients. She has worked on issues arising from business succession planning, family trusts, shareholder arrangements, and wealth transfer strategies for family and business assets’ preservation and protection. She has assisted business owners with developing bespoke structures supporting growth, facilitating ownership transitions, and preparing businesses for future generations. The Lexpert -ranked lawyer has handled corporate restructurings and estate freezes as well. Lexpert included her in its 2026 Special Edition on Canada’s Leading Mergers & Acquisitions Lawyers . Muth spent over seven years at Pallett Valo, where she made partner in 2024. While there, she tackled matters involving incorporation, contracts, mergers and acquisitions, asset and share purchases and sales, and wealth preservation, according to LinkedIn . She was once an associate at McMaster, McIntyre & Smyth, LLP. She also logged a stint at Templeman Menninga LLP, where she was an articling student and associate lawyer. Muth is the public affairs liaison of the Ontario Bar Association’s business law section, of which she was previously chair. As liaison, she consults on legislative reforms, such as changes to Ontario’s Business Corporations Act with regard to transparency register requirements. Moreover, she is the secretary of the Society of Trust and Estate Practitioners’ Toronto branch and a member-at-large of the Ontario Bar Association’s sexual orientation and gender identity community section. She contributes to Ontario Bar Association, the Law Society of Ontario, the Canadian Tax Foundation programs as a speaker and author on business succession planning, corporate reorganizations, trusts, estates, and governance matters. Muth taught law and entrepreneurship and business law courses in 2018 and 2019, respectively, at Wilfrid Laurier University. She tackled intellectual property law, advertising and marketing law, commercial financing, and government regulation of competition, as well as contract law, Canadian legal institutions, tort law, business associations, and business transactions. She was called to the Ontario bar in 2015. She obtained her JD from the Queen’s University School of Law in 2014. She is fluent in English and Romanian. https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjhvkzt.text: The White House has not officially disclosed the reason for CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s unusual visit to Moscow on Tuesday, but overnight Wednesday into Thursday, at least some of the theories surrounding the trip gained support. The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. intelligence chief traveled to the Russian capital to warn the Kremlin against attacking NATO. Politico published a similar report, adding that Ratcliffe also pressed Moscow to reduce its military and economic support for Iran. The Journal’s report was based on people briefed on the surprise visit, Ratcliffe’s first to Russia as CIA director. Earlier this month, the newspaper reported that according to updated Western intelligence assessments, Russia could seek to test NATO’s commitment to its members by attacking an alliance country in the coming years. Leaders of the Baltic states — Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia — have repeatedly voiced concern that the region could become a flashpoint between Russia and the West. The report also said U.S. officials are concerned that Russian President Vladimir Putin, under growing pressure in the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, could launch an attack ranging from a cyber operation to a limited military incursion, most likely against one of the Baltic states. Politico, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported that Ratcliffe warned Russian officials in Moscow not to escalate confrontation with U.S. NATO allies, with a particular emphasis on the Baltic states. One person who spoke to Politico and a British official said the CIA director also used the visit to press Russia to reduce its economic and military support for Iran. The British official said Ratcliffe raised the issue following U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s threat to intensify sanctions against countries that refuse to sever economic ties with Iran. According to the official, Ratcliffe made clear that Russia should stop sharing weapons and defense technology with Iran and advised Moscow not to “overreact” if it is affected by U.S. sanctions. Neither Politico nor The Wall Street Journal said whether Ratcliffe met directly with Putin. On the day of the visit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov initially said he did not know who had arrived in Moscow aboard a U.S. military C-17 transport aircraft. He later confirmed that the visitor was the CIA director and that Putin was aware of the trip. Peskov said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin but came for an “interagency” meeting and that the Russian president was briefed on the talks. The Kremlin has confirmed that Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials during the rare visit. One person who spoke to Politico said the meeting was intended “primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states.” Under Article 5 of the NATO treaty, an attack on one alliance member is considered an attack on all, obligating members to come to the defense of the country under attack. Russia, however, has for years used methods such as cyberattacks and sabotage to harm other countries and carry out hostile operations on their territory without triggering the clause. In recent weeks, various Russian figures, including former President Dmitry Medvedev, have intensified threats of escalation against “the West,” including threats against NATO. Medvedev, along with hard-line television host Vladimir Solovyov and other propagandists, frequently justifies such rhetoric by claiming Russia is already “fighting NATO in Ukraine.” The White House declined to comment and instead referred to remarks President Donald Trump made earlier in an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck. Trump described Ratcliffe’s trip as “semi-routine” and shifted the discussion to the war in Ukraine. “Something may come out of it,” Trump said of the visit. “We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.” The CIA declined to comment. The last known visit to Russia by a CIA director took place in November 2021, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. During that trip, then-CIA Director William Burns warned Putin against attacking Ukraine. Unusual strike in Donetsk Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine continued to strike targets deep behind each other’s front lines. Explosions were heard overnight in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, while authorities also reported a Russian attack on an “industrial facility” in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown. The head of the city’s military administration said Russia used ballistic missiles and that two people were wounded, but provided no further details. Hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a relatively unusual strike, apparently using cruise missiles, on the Russian-occupied city of Donetsk. No Ukrainian official claimed responsibility for the attack, but extensive destruction was documented in the area. Ukrainian Telegram channels reported that the target may have been the headquarters of the Russian military’s 51st Army. The Kremlin-appointed governor of the Donetsk region did not provide details about the target and said only that several civilians had been wounded. Earlier, the Russian newspaper Izvestia reported that 10 people were killed in the unusual strike, but the report was later removed. One possible explanation is that the Ukrainian reports were accurate and Russian authorities did not want to disclose that military forces had been hit. Russian state media, which operate under tight restrictions, reported that a shopping center called Donetsk City had been struck. An Izvestia correspondent, however, reported that the missiles landed “near” the shopping center building, and images of the destruction did not show the mall itself.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: The Hawk T2 aircraft was trailing smoke before it crashed near houses and agricultural buildings, sending a fireball into the sky. Photograph: John Heyworth/Facebook View image in fullscreen The Hawk T2 aircraft was trailing smoke before it crashed near houses and agricultural buildings, sending a fireball into the sky. Photograph: John Heyworth/Facebook Royal Air Force RAF jet crashes and explodes in Anglesey moments after pilots eject Witness says T2 Hawk aircraft, which was being used for a training flight, ‘was basically on fire’ on takeoff Harry Cockburn Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.36 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An RAF jet crashed and exploded moments after two pilots ejected during a training flight over Anglesey (Ynys Môn) in north Wales on Wednesday. The aircraft, a Hawk T2, had just taken off from RAF Valley on the west of the island when the incident occurred, witnesses said. RAF pilots eject from training plane before crash Both pilots parachuted to the ground and were reportedly treated for minor injuries. A video of the crash shows the aircraft appearing to climb unevenly before the pilots eject. The plane then nosedives towards the ground while trailing smoke and crashing near houses and agricultural buildings, sending an enormous fireball into the sky. An RAF spokesperson said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.” The site of the crash, at Pencarnisiog, is less than two miles from the airbase. RAF Valley is home to the air force’s No 4 Flying Training School, which trains fighter pilots using Hawk T2 and Texan T1 aircraft. A spokesperson for North Wales fire and rescue service said: “Crews and officers attended an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues from Royal Air Force , North Wales police, Welsh ambulance service and Wales air ambulance. The fire is now under control.” They added: “Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.” Due to the crash, local train lines were closed and replacement buses were running between Bangor and Holyhead. View image in fullscreen The jet, moments before it crashed. Photograph: John Heyworth/Facebook Pete Bennett, a local resident, told Wales Live it appeared the plane was in trouble as soon as it left the runway. He said: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble. Right on takeoff there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire. “As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch – like the pilot was trying to gain altitude. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear, loud bangs. It was probably at around 800ft at this point. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.” He said the explosion caused a “huge wall of fire and black smoke”. He added: “The aircrew came down around halfway between the runway and where the plane crashed, which I’m guessing was around a mile inland from RAF Valley.” The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said in a post on X : “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.” North Wales police said: “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.” Explore more on these topics Royal Air Force Military Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Family Handout/PA Suffolk NHS trust removes 10 staff from duty over Noah Woods data breach East Suffolk and North Essex NHS trust apologises after illicit access of medical records of toddler who died in Brantham Helena Horton Sun 27 Sep 2026 03.51 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 05.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An NHS trust has apologised after the medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods were accessed by unauthorised people after his disappearance. Noah was found dead in a pond in Brantham, Suffolk , after going missing from a playground. More than 1,300 members of the public joined a search for the boy before police discovered his body. A spokesperson for East Suffolk and North Essex NHS foundation trust said 10 employees had been “removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded”. The trust said in a statement that disciplinary action was being explored as a result. Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at the trust, said: “We have apologised unreservedly to Noah Woods’ family for the extra anguish this breach of trust has caused them at an already devastating time.” He added that unauthorised access of patient data was “completely unacceptable” and said the matter had been reported to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). Mansfield added: “As soon as we became aware of concerns that Noah’s medical records may have been viewed inappropriately, we launched an urgent internal investigation. Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason.” The chief executive of NHS England , Sir Jim Mackey, said on Friday that NHS staff would be suspended immediately if found snooping on patients’ records for unauthorised reasons. He said: “We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough.” There have been previous cases of NHS staff looking at patient records in high-profile cases, including the 2023 Nottingham attacks and the 2024 Southport dance class knife attack . An inquest heard this week that Woods escaped from the park “through a gap in the fence”. He became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk constabulary said. Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk constabulary said his death was not being treated as suspicious. After the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday, Noah’s family said they would like him to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”. In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.” Noah’s father, Rhys Woods , paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.” Explore more on these topics Suffolk NHS England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: People living near the chip shop have referred to the ‘TikTok queue’ that builds outside the premises on Runstraat. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian View image in fullscreen People living near the chip shop have referred to the ‘TikTok queue’ that builds outside the premises on Runstraat. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian Netherlands ‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court Neighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats Senay Boztas in Amsterdam. Photographs by Judith Jockel Sun 4 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 06.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok . View image in fullscreen ‘It has polluted the whole area’ … Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives near to Fabel Friet. On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop. “We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.” Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size. “What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.” In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business. View image in fullscreen Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff in the case. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling. The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations . “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.” View image in fullscreen The queue outside Fabel Friet, which occupies a small premises. Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.” View image in fullscreen Herring gulls have been attracted to the area by the leftovers and waste. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.” Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said. Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.” View image in fullscreen A customer with a portion of Fabel Friet’s signature fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Photograph: Judith Jockel/The Guardian Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.” View image in fullscreen ‘I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours’ … Natalie Stübben. Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.” Explore more on these topics Netherlands TikTok Europe Food & drink industry Chips (french fries) features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
